intro.en: Systematic bedside approach to paediatric general physical examination, vital signs, temperature patterns, pulse palpation, blood pressure measurement, and respiratory dynamics.

title.en: Paediatric examination kit and clinical preparation

items.summary: Core equipment required at the bedside and initial hygienic measures before commencing a comprehensive physical examination in children.

blocks.title: Initial examiner preparation
bullets: Wash hands thoroughly following standard clinical infection control protocols before approaching the patient.
Rub hands together to warm palms and fingers so cold contact does not distress the infant.
Clean stethoscope diaphragms and examination tools prior to patient contact.

blocks.title: Essential bedside tools
bullets: Paediatric stethoscope with appropriately sized bell and diaphragm.
Pen torch for inspecting oral cavity, pupils, and throat mucosa.
Non-stretchable flexible measuring tape for head and circumference charting.
Wooden tongue spatula for pharyngeal inspection.
Knee percussion hammer and tuning forks with frequencies of 216 Hz and 512 Hz.
Dedicated neurological examination kit for assessing sensory and motor responses.

blocks.title: Developmental assessment items
bullets: Red wooden or plastic ring suspended by a string for tracking fixation and visual pursuit.
Set of 9 red wooden cubes measuring one inch each for evaluating grasp and stacking skills.
Small paper pellets to assess fine pincer grasp and pellet retrieval.
Colourful picture book to elicit vocalisation, pointing, and naming.
Small drinking cup and metal spoon to observe feeding skills and interactive motor play.

viva.q: Why is it mandatory to warm your hands before examining a paediatric patient?
viva.a: Cold hands trigger crying, abdominal guarding, and tachycardia, which invalidate resting vital sign measurements and abdominal palpation.

viva.q: Which tuning fork frequencies should be kept in a paediatric clinical kit?
viva.a: Frequencies of 216 Hz and 512 Hz are maintained for testing bone conduction, sensory vibration, and acoustic acuity.

viva.q: What specific tools in the examination tray test fine motor development in an infant?
viva.a: Nine red wooden cubes assess tower building, while small paper pellets test the development of an inferior or neat pincer grasp.

title.en: Body temperature measurement and fever evaluation

items.summary: Site-specific diagnostic thresholds for fever, hyperpyrexia definitions, physiological vitals coupling, and classical paediatric fever patterns.

blocks.title: Diagnostic temperature thresholds
bullets: Fever is clinically established when core rectal temperature exceeds 38 deg C (100.4 deg F).
Hyperpyrexia represents extreme core hyperthermia defined by a temperature surpassing 41.5 deg C (107 deg F).
Physiological site hierarchy follows rectal (38 deg C or 100.4 deg F) greater than oral (37.5 deg C or 99.5 deg F) greater than axillary (37.2 deg C or 99 deg F), remembered as ROA.

blocks.title: Classical fever curves
bullets: Continuous fever maintains diurnal fluctuations under 1 deg C and never returns to baseline.
Remittent fever fluctuates by more than 1 deg C within 24 hours without touching baseline, classically seen in enteric fever.
Intermittent fever spikes periodically and returns completely to baseline between paroxysms.

blocks.title: Intermittent fever variations and specific syndromes
bullets: Quotidian pattern recurs on a daily basis, characteristically seen in juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA).
Tertian pattern recurs every alternate day on day 1 and day 3, typical of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
Quartan pattern recurs every third day on day 1 and day 4, classical for Plasmodium malariae.
Pel-Ebstein fever displays cyclical waves of pyrexia followed by afebrile intervals, seen in Hodgkin lymphoma and brucellosis.
Saddleback biphasic fever features initial high spikes, a brief afebrile remission, and a secondary rise, classical for dengue.

blocks.title: Temperature effects on vital parameters
bullets: Each single degree Fahrenheit rise in body temperature elevates pulse rate by 10 beats per minute.
Each single degree Fahrenheit rise raises respiratory rate by 4 breaths per minute.
Expected physiological ratio of pulse rate to respiratory rate is 4:1.

viva.q: What core temperature reading defines hyperpyrexia in children?
viva.a: A core body temperature greater than 41.5 deg C or 107 deg F defines clinical hyperpyrexia.

viva.q: How does fever quantitatively modify pulse and respiratory rates in children?
viva.a: For each 1 deg F elevation, the pulse rate rises by 10 beats per minute and respiratory rate increases by 4 breaths per minute.

viva.q: What distinguishes tertian from quartan intermittent fever paroxysms?
viva.a: Tertian spikes occur on day 1 and day 3 as in Plasmodium vivax, whereas quartan spikes occur on day 1 and day 4 in Plasmodium malariae.

title.en: Arterial pulse assessment and tachycardia thresholds

items.summary: Systematic three-finger palpation method for peripheral pulses, assessment of rhythm and character, and age-stratified criteria for tachycardia.

blocks.title: Three-finger palpation technique
bullets: Count the arterial pulse over one full minute by palpating the radial artery against the distal radius.
Position the index finger to evaluate rate and detect rhythm regularities or irregularities.
Rest the middle finger over the pulse point to assess pulse volume.
Utilise the ring finger proximally to obliterate the arterial pulse and examine vessel wall consistency.

blocks.title: Age-stratified tachycardia cutoffs
bullets: Newborn (NB): resting pulse rate exceeding 160 beats per minute indicates tachycardia.
Infants under 1 year: pulse rate exceeding 140 beats per minute defines tachycardia.
Children aged 1 to 5 years: pulse rate exceeding 120 beats per minute indicates tachycardia.
Children over 5 years: pulse rate exceeding 100 beats per minute denotes tachycardia.
In young infants, direct precordial auscultation of heart sounds is preferred over peripheral palpation.

blocks.title: Pulse qualities and comparative assessment
bullets: Rhythm evaluated at the radial artery is classified as regular or irregular.
Volume at the radial artery is graded as normal, high bounding, or low volume.
Character evaluated at the carotid artery identifies pulsus alternans, collapsing pulse, or dicrotic pulse.
Check for radio-femoral delay to detect coarctation of aorta, where femoral pulsations normally precede radial pulses.
Palpate peripheral pulses bilaterally including brachial, radial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.

viva.q: What are the roles of the three examining fingers during radial pulse palpation?
viva.a: The index finger evaluates rate and rhythm, the middle finger assesses pulse volume, and the ring finger obliterates flow to assess vessel wall texture.

viva.q: What pulse rate cutoffs define tachycardia in infants and children over 5 years?
viva.a: Tachycardia is defined by a rate exceeding 140 per minute in infants under 1 year, and exceeding 100 per minute in children over 5 years.

viva.q: What clinical condition is suspected when radio-femoral delay is detected?
viva.a: Radio-femoral delay indicates coarctation of aorta; under normal conditions femoral pulsations are felt simultaneously or slightly before radial pulses.

title.en: Paediatric blood pressure measurement and cuff selection

items.summary: Selection criteria for sphygmomanometer cuff bladder size, age-specific reference values, estimation formulas, and Korotkoff sound interpretation.

blocks.title: Cuff selection rules and measurement technique
bullets: Inflatable bladder width must span at least two thirds of the upper arm length between acromion and olecranon.
Under-sized cuffs produce falsely elevated blood pressure readings due to inadequate pressure transmission.
Over-sized cuffs yield falsely depressed blood pressure values across clinical measurements.
Plot recorded systolic and diastolic values on paediatric centile charts matched to height percentiles.
Readings exceeding the 95th percentile establish the clinical diagnosis of paediatric hypertension.

blocks.title: Age-stratified normal values and cuff dimensions
Bedside formula estimations for children over 1 year
bullets: Upper threshold of systolic blood pressure equals 90 plus twice the chronological age in years.
Upper threshold of diastolic blood pressure equals 60 plus twice the chronological age in years.
Lower threshold of systolic blood pressure (hypotension cutoff) equals 70 plus twice the chronological age in years.

blocks.title: Korotkoff sound phases and special clinical situations
bullets: Phase 1 produces clear tapping sounds signifying systolic blood pressure.
Phase 2 consists of soft murmurs, progressing to phase 3 where murmurs become noticeably louder.
Phase 4 marks distinct muffling of sounds.
Phase 5 represents complete disappearance of sound, corresponding to standard diastolic blood pressure in children.
In aortic regurgitation, phase 4 muffling represents diastolic pressure because sounds may persist down to 0 mm Hg.
Measure blood pressure in all four limbs in suspected coarctation or congenital heart disease.
Record standing blood pressure to identify orthostatic postural drops.

viva.q: What rule governs the width of a blood pressure cuff bladder in paediatrics?
viva.a: The inflatable bladder width must cover at least two thirds of the child upper arm length to prevent falsely high or low readings.

viva.q: How is the upper limit of normal systolic blood pressure calculated for a child over 1 year?
viva.a: The upper systolic limit is estimated using the formula 90 plus twice the child chronological age in years.

viva.q: Why is Korotkoff phase 4 used instead of phase 5 in children with aortic regurgitation?
viva.a: In aortic regurgitation, sounds may be heard down to 0 mm Hg, making phase 4 muffling the accurate surrogate for diastolic pressure.

title.en: Respiratory rate assessment, tachypnoea thresholds, and breathing patterns

items.summary: Resting respiratory rate ranges by age, World Health Organization tachypnoea criteria, developmental breathing types, and abnormal respiratory rhythms.

blocks.title: Developmental type of respiration
bullets: Newborn infants exhibit predominantly abdominal breathing.
Children under 5 years and females exhibit thoraco-abdominal respiration.
Children over 5 years display abdomino-thoracic breathing movements.

blocks.title: Depth and variations in respiratory excursion
bullets: Normal breathing cycles display regular inspiration followed by expiration and an end-expiratory pause.
Shallow breathing occurs with central depression from narcotic poisoning.
Deep and rapid Kussmaul respiration is characteristic of metabolic acidosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.

blocks.title: Rhythm patterns and periodic breathing
bullets: Respiratory rhythm is evaluated as regular or irregular during quiet observation.
Cheyne-Stokes breathing in cardiac failure features cycles of hyperpnoea and hypopnoea followed by apnoea.
Biot breathing in raised intracranial pressure features irregular apnoeic pauses alternating with 4 to 5 equal depth breaths.
Periodic breathing in neonates is physiological when apnoeic episodes last under 20 seconds without cyanosis or bradycardia.
Inspect for recruitment of accessory respiratory muscles including intercostal, subcostal, and suprasternal retractions.

viva.q: What are the WHO fast breathing thresholds for infants under 2 months and children aged 1 to 5 years?
viva.a: Fast breathing is defined as greater than 60 breaths per minute under 2 months, and greater than 40 breaths per minute between 1 and 5 years.

viva.q: When is periodic breathing considered physiological in a neonate?
viva.a: Periodic breathing is benign if apnoeic pauses last under 20 seconds and occur without concomitant bradycardia or cyanosis.

viva.q: What respiratory pattern is typical of severe metabolic acidosis?
viva.a: Kussmaul breathing, characterized by deep, rapid, and unlaboured hyperventilation, is typical of metabolic acidosis such as diabetic ketoacidosis.
